recipe.history:
Switzerland's two great melting cheeses — Emmentaler and Gruyère — represent twin peaks of a cheesemaking tradition that stretches back to the high Alpine pastures of the Middle Ages. Emmentaler, produced in the Emme Valley of the canton of Bern since the thirteenth century, is the archetypal 'Swiss cheese' of popular imagination: pale yellow, elastic, threaded with the iconic holes (called 'eyes') produced by Propionibacterium freudenreichii during aging. Gruyère, made in the canton of Fribourg since at least the twelfth century, is its more assertive cousin — denser, darker, with fewer eyes and a complex flavor profile that moves through sweet, nutty, and earthy notes as it ages, developing a crystalline, almost savory depth after eighteen months or more. Both cheeses were developed to preserve the abundance of summer Alpine milk through long winters, and both carry an AOP (Appellation d'Origine Protégée) designation that ties them legally and culturally to the landscapes that made them. Together, they represent the full chromatic range of Swiss dairy artisanship: Emmentaler's mild creaminess and Gruyère's funky, assertive richness.

Swiss cheese — predominantly Emmentaler in the American imagination — crossed the Atlantic with the waves of German and Swiss immigrants who settled in the Midwest in the nineteenth century. Wisconsin and Ohio cheesemakers began producing domestic versions by the 1850s, and by the mid-twentieth century, 'Swiss' had become one of the standard diner cheese options, nestled comfortably between American and provolone on any laminated menu. The burger industry adopted it particularly for its clean, nutty melt, which doesn't dominate the beef the way sharp cheddar can. The Swiss-ter Act 2 Burger goes further, doubling down on the Swiss tradition by layering both Emmentaler and Gruyère — letting the mild creaminess of one and the complex savoriness of the other build a cheese experience that truly rewards the second act. Two cheeses, one vision, maximum Alpine drama.

I spent a semester studying abroad near Lausanne in my early twenties, and I ate Gruyère nearly every day — on bread, melted into fondue, shaved over salads — and I remember the specific shock of the first time I had a truly aged Gruyère, maybe twenty-four months, purchased from a fromagerie in the covered market. It smelled faintly of cellar and hay and something almost meaty, and when I tasted it I sat down because my legs went slightly unreliable. That memory has colored every cheese decision I've made in a kitchen since. When I came home and started building burgers with Swiss cheeses, I knew immediately that using just one was a compromise — Emmentaler alone was too mild, Gruyère alone too assertive — and that the only honest answer was both, stacked in sequence so that each patty carries the full conversation of Swiss dairy culture.

The philosophy of medium rare cookery begins with a simple acknowledgment: beef at its best is a living system of fat, protein, and moisture, and heat is a force that either unlocks or destroys. At 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, the proteins have tightened just enough to give structure without squeezing out the juices, the fat has begun its inward journey of self-basting, and the myoglobin — the protein that gives beef its red color and its iron-forward flavor — remains present and vibrant. Beyond 140 degrees, you are cooking through the point of no return: moisture flees, fat congeals, flavor flattens. For the Swiss-ter Act 2 Burger specifically, medium rare matters because both Emmentaler and Gruyère melt differently and at slightly different temperatures; a still-warm, yielding patty allows both cheeses to melt at their own pace, creating layers of flavor rather than a single congealed slab. To cook this burger to well done would be an act of culinary self-sabotage. Medium rare is the only correct answer.
ingredients: 480g bread flour, plus more for dusting
1 large egg beaten with 1 tbsp water, for egg wash
900g freshly ground beef (75% chuck, 25% short rib)
softened unsalted butter, for toasting buns
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Combine flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in the bowl of a stand mixer with the dough hook. Add warm milk, water, and the whole egg; mix on low until combined, about 2 minutes.
2. Add softened butter one tablespoon at a time on medium speed. Increase to medium-high and knead until smooth and elastic, about 8 to 9 minutes.

3. Transfer to a lightly oiled bowl, cover, and let rise until doubled, 1 to 1.5 hours. Punch down, divide into 6 portions (about 140g each), shape into tight rounds, and place on parchment-lined baking sheets. Cover and proof 45 minutes.
4. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush buns with egg wash, sprinkle with poppy seeds, and bake until deep golden, 18 to 20 minutes. Cool on a wire rack.
5. Make the Swiss mustard aioli: Whisk mayonnaise, both mustards, honey, and vinegar together until smooth. Refrigerate until needed.

6. Cook the mushrooms: Melt butter with olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add mushrooms in a single layer; do not stir for 3 minutes to allow browning. Stir, add garlic and white wine, and cook until liquid evaporates and mushrooms are deeply caramelized, about 8 more minutes. Season with salt and pepper. Set aside.

7. Form the patties: Divide beef into 6 portions (about 150g each). Shape gently into 4-inch patties, 3/4 inch thick, with a center dimple. Season both sides generously with kosher salt and black pepper just before cooking.
8. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet or griddle over high heat until smoking. Cook patties undisturbed for 3 minutes on the first side.
9. Flip the patties. Lay 1 to 2 slices of Emmentaler directly on the patty, then layer Gruyère slices on top of the Emmentaler. Cook for 2 to 2.5 more minutes.

10. Add a splash of water to the skillet and cover immediately to steam-melt the cheeses for 30 seconds. The internal temperature must reach 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) — this is medium rare, and it is the only acceptable doneness. Rest patties on a rack for 3 minutes.
11. Toast the buns: Butter the cut sides and toast in the skillet butter-side down over medium heat until golden and crisp, about 1 minute.

12. Assemble: Spread Swiss mustard aioli on both bun halves. Lay arugula on the bottom bun, then a tomato slice, then a few dill pickle chips. Place the double-Swiss-covered patty on top. Spoon a generous amount of caramelized mushrooms over the cheese. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately.
